analysis.one_liner: Requires nursing homes that take Medicare or Medicaid to meet minimum daily nurse staffing levels.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 70 House Democrats and the Independent, never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written federal minimum nurse staffing standards into Medicare and Medicaid rules, using staffing levels the Department of Health and Human Services itself identified in a 2002 report to Congress: roughly 2.4 to 2.8 hours of aide care per resident per day plus a set amount of licensed and registered nurse time. Facilities would have had to post how much nursing care residents actually received, and government survey teams could examine facilities' financial records to check whether public payments were being spent on care. To soften the blow, the bill also raised federal Medicaid payments to states by 1.5 percentage points and restored an older rule (the Boren amendment) that required states to pay nursing homes rates tied to the actual cost of care.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents, who would have gotten more hands-on care per day, and their families, who would gain public information about each facility's actual staffing. Nurses and aides would benefit from higher demand for their work.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and their families

how_it_helps.text: Facilities receiving Medicare or Medicaid payments would have to meet minimum staffing levels of 2.4 to 2.8 hours of certified nurse aide care per resident per day, plus 1.15 to 1.3 hours from licensed and registered nurses, based on levels HHS identified in its March 2002 report to Congress.
Only staff actually providing direct nursing care could be counted toward the ratios — administrative, kitchen, and housekeeping workers would not qualify.
Facilities would have to publicly post the average hours of nursing care residents received each of the past four quarters, letting families compare facilities before choosing one.

Government inspection teams could examine a facility's financial records to determine whether Medicare and Medicaid payments were being used on resident care, and could include trained accountants and auditors on the team.

States would receive a permanent 1.5 percentage point increase in the federal Medicaid matching rate starting in fiscal 2004, and a restored payment rule would push states toward paying nursing homes rates based on the actual cost of care.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home operators, who would bear the cost of hiring additional aides and nurses; and federal taxpayers, who would fund the higher Medicaid matching rate and, indirectly, higher Medicaid rates to facilities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home operators and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Nursing labor is the largest single cost in nursing home care, so the staffing floors would have required significant new spending by facilities, which could strain smaller and rural operators or lead them to seek payment increases.

The bill's answer to those costs was more public money: a permanent 1.5 point increase in the federal Medicaid match plus a restored cost-based payment rule, meaning federal and state taxpayers would absorb a substantial share of the added cost.

The bill let the HHS Secretary delay full compliance for up to five years with gradually increasing intermediate standards if immediate compliance was judged infeasible, so benefits would arrive slowly for some residents.

The bill itself states that meeting the staffing ratios alone would not satisfy the underlying requirement to provide care that maintains each resident's well-being, acknowledging that staffing minimums are a floor, not a guarantee of quality.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is substantial and well-grounded: the staffing thresholds came from HHS's own multi-year study of what care residents need, and public staffing data plus financial audits address real, documented problems in the industry. The costs — higher facility labor bills and more federal Medicaid spending — are real, but the bill anticipated them with payment increases and a phase-in option. Its main design weakness is that more federal money would flow to facilities without a strict requirement that it be spent on staffing; the audit provision was the check on that, and it was only permissive.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to a Health subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the bill on October 21, 2003, with 41 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
It eventually gathered 69 cosponsors — 68 Democrats and one Independent — and no Republicans.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced.
Six days later it was sent to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and no further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the 108th Congress.
The bill expired on January 3, 2005, when the 108th Congress ended, without any committee or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators came out ahead: they avoided a federal staffing mandate, public staffing disclosure, and financial audits of their use of Medicare and Medicaid payments. Residents and families gained nothing from the bill's death, though taxpayers also avoided its added cost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home operators who faced no new staffing rules

sides.party_line_note: All 70 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the one Independent; no Republican signed on, and the House never voted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have required facilities to hire significantly more nursing staff and open their books to auditors, but it also would have sent them more money: a permanent federal Medicaid match increase and a restored cost-based payment rule. Operators would have faced higher labor costs and closer scrutiny while receiving higher public payments.
Minimum staffing ratios translate directly into demand for aides, licensed nurses, and registered nurses, and the bill barred counting non-care staff toward the ratios.
A permanent 1.5 percentage point increase in the federal Medicaid match would have shifted part of state nursing home Medicaid costs to the federal government.
